title: The 7-Month Referee Lag
script: By the time the news officially declares a recession, it's already seventy percent over. You've probably heard the textbook rule: two quarters of negative GDP. Except in America, recessions aren't called by a formula. They're decided by a private committee of eight economists. Because economic data takes months to verify, it takes them an average of seven full months just to make the announcement. In 1980, they didn't declare the recession until it was literally over. And in 2020, they declared it months after the market had already bottomed. This creates a lethal psychological trap. By the time everyday people panic about headline news, smart money is already buying the recovery. Never trade on delayed news. Tap the related video below to see fifty years of data.

title: The Lead-Lag Paradox
script: The single best day to buy stocks in fifty years happened when the news was screaming the world was ending. Most people assume the stock market will keep falling until the economic data improves. The data proves the exact opposite. The stock market doesn't trade on today. It prices corporate profits six to nine months into the future. Across five decades of recessions, the market consistently bottoms out three to five months before the recession is even close to over. On March 9th, 2009, unemployment was skyrocketing and banks were failing. Yet that exact day was the generational bottom, surging over sixty percent in twelve months. If you wait for the news to report that the coast is clear, you miss the most profitable rally of the entire economic cycle. Stop following headline panic. title: The 5-Year Jobs Trap
script: The average recession lasts just ten months. But getting your job back takes five full years. When you're living through a downturn, the constant barrage of negative news makes it feel permanent. Yet fifty years of data reveals the average recession lasts just ten point four months. Economic expansions average over five years. Asset prices rebound in months. But employment behaves like an elevator on the way down, and the stairs on the way up. Mass layoffs strike in weeks. But returning to pre-recession employment levels takes an average of three to five years. That's why everyday families still feel intense pressure long after Wall Street celebrates new record highs. Understand the real rules of the economic cycle. Tap the related video below for the full episode.
